Saturday, 11 October 2030, 9 a.m., at the Estaque music school in Marseille. The planting of the first lime tree is scheduled for 11 o’clock, in the presence of the minister. But the mistral has got up, with gusts of 90 km/h. Julien wants to send Odile indoors.
Odile, there are gusts of ninety kilometres an hour. You should stay inside.
Old as I may be, I’m not made of sugar. I saw far worse storms on Henri’s ship.
Although you’re right, Dr Martin made me promise to keep an eye on you.
Dr Martin is in Lyon. And whatever he may have told me, I carried this lime tree on my lap for three hours on the train. I’ll plant it.
Madame is right, Mr Moreau. Here in Marseille, whatever the wind, we don’t back down. The mistral is an old friend.
An old friend that might rip out a one-metre tree!
Not if we give it a good stake. I’ve planted olive trees here all my life. Wherever you put them, they hold, as long as you tie them well.
You see? Even the olive trees are on my side.
And the minister? He arrives at eleven. Even if we did plant the tree, he might not hear a word of his own speech.
So much the better. Speeches are carried off by the wind. Trees stay.
Mr Benhamou, you talk like my husband. He would have loved this place. Whoever the children who play here may be, they’ll have the most beautiful view in the world.
(sighs) All right. You win. But you put on the shawl, and you hold my arm.
Conductor though you are, Julien, you won’t conduct the wind. But all right for the arm.
“Kwa-kuh” in both cases. Only the spelling and meaning tell them apart!
Malgré le vent, nous planterons l’arbre.
Même si le vent souffle, nous planterons l’arbre.
“Malgré que” + subjunctive is used in speech, but purists consider it wrong. In writing use “bien que” or “quoique”.
They sound the same, but mean different things:
Si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit, appelle.
Tip: if you can replace it with “bien que”, write QUOIQUE. If it means “whatever thing”, write QUOI QUE.
3. Où que, qui que, quel que soit
These expressions generalise: wherever, whoever, whatever. All take the SUBJUNCTIVE:
Wherever you put them, olive trees hold.
Whoever the children may be, they’ll have a beautiful view.
Whatever the wind, we don’t back down.
“Quel” AGREES with the noun after “soit”: quel que soit le vent, quelle que soit la météo, quels que soient les risques, quelles que soient les conditions.
J’ai beau être vieille, je viendrai. (= old as I may be)
Quand bien même il pleuvrait, je resterais.
Tout chef d’orchestre que vous êtes, …

On Friday 10 October, on the two o’clock TGV to Marseille, there was a passenger the whole carriage was looking at. She was an old lady with white hair, a shawl over her shoulders, holding a little tree in a pot on her lap. She hadn’t let go of it once since Lyon. When the train braked, she clutched the pot to her, the way you hold a child.

After an hour, a little girl sitting across the aisle couldn’t resist any longer. She came over and asked Odile why she was travelling with a tree. Odile told her the story: the bench, the kiss, the waltz, the sailor, the sixty years of waiting. The little girl listened to the end without moving. Then she asked if she could water the lime tree with her bottle of water.

Odile agreed, on condition that she only poured a little sip. The little girl poured the water with extreme concentration, as if she were taking part in a religious ceremony. When she went back to her seat, her mother thanked Odile in a low voice. “She’ll talk about nothing else for weeks,” she said. “Thank you.” Odile smiled. The lime tree had already started its work.

In Marseille the weather was mild and the sky a perfect blue. But during the night the wind got up. In their little hotel in L’Estaque, the shutters banged until morning. Julien barely slept. He spent the night imagining the lime tree torn up, carried off towards the sea, before the minister’s eyes. Odile slept like a baby. Storms were an old acquaintance of hers.

On Saturday morning, the mistral was blowing in gusts of ninety kilometres an hour. The palm trees in the harbour were bending. The boats strained at their moorings. Julien tried to persuade Odile to stay inside. However much he insisted, invoked Dr Martin, talked about caution, it was no use. Odile replied that she wasn’t made of sugar, and Mr Benhamou agreed with her.

Mr Benhamou had brought an extraordinary stake: an old olive-wood post, gnarled and grey, from his grandfather’s garden. “It held three olive trees upright for sixty years,” he explained. “It’ll hold a Lyon lime tree.” They dug the hole together, Julien, Mr Benhamou and two big boys from the neighbourhood, while Odile supervised the operations, sitting on a chair, wrapped up in her shawl.

At ten the school children arrived. There were about twenty of them, aged six to fourteen, with all sorts of instruments: two violins, a guitar, three ukuleles, a dented trumpet and a drum made from an old can. Mr Benhamou had taught them the waltz all through September. They had fixed their scores to music stands with clothes pegs, so the wind wouldn’t carry them off.

The minister arrived at eleven sharp, in a black car, with three advisers and a photographer. He was a man of about fifty, with grey hair, who seemed genuinely happy to be there. As he got out of the car, a gust nearly tore his papers from his hands. He looked at his notes, then at the sky, then put his notes in his pocket.

His speech lasted three minutes instead of ten. He spoke of every child’s right to music, wherever they live and whoever their parents are. He said, smiling, that minister though he was, he couldn’t play the waltz. Then he gave the floor to “the most important person of the morning”: Odile.

Odile stood up. She refused Julien’s arm. She took the shovel, which was almost as tall as she was, and threw three shovelfuls of earth at the foot of the lime tree, one for Henri, one for Hélène, and one, she said later, for all those who wait. Then she turned towards the sea and whistled the first three notes of the waltz.

The children struck up the rest, with their violins, their ukuleles and their can drum. It sounded nothing like the La Duchère orchestra, or the Philharmonie. It was out of tune, joyful, chaotic, and the wind carried off half the notes. But it was Henri’s waltz, played by the children of L’Estaque, facing the sea, a few kilometres from the terrace where Julien’s grandmother had danced all her life.

It was at that moment that a gust stronger than the others arrived. The lime tree bent almost to the ground. Everyone held their breath. The minister took a step forward, as if to catch it. But the old olive post held. When the gust had passed, the little tree straightened up, slowly, with all its leaves. The children let out a cry of victory.

“You see,” said Mr Benhamou, laughing. “It’s only been here ten minutes, and it already has a Marseille accent. Whatever happens, that one won’t leave again.” The minister’s photographer took a photo at that precise moment: the lime tree straightening, Odile leaning on her shovel, and the sea behind, white with foam. The photo would be on the front page of La Provence the next day.

In the afternoon, despite the wind, Odile asked Julien to take her to Les Goudes. She wanted to see the house with the blue shutters he had told her so much about. They sat on the steps in front of the empty terrace. The shutters were closed; the house was let to tourists in summer and empty the rest of the year. Odile looked at the sea for a long time without speaking.

“Henri came through here, you know,” she said at last. “In 1971, the year we met. His ship called at Marseille. Perhaps he walked past this house. Perhaps he heard your grandfather playing the accordion.” Julien said nothing. There was nothing to say. The world was decidedly much smaller than people thought.

They got back to Lyon on Sunday evening. On Monday morning, Odile didn’t open her door to listen to Rose-Hélène’s harmonica. Ioana knocked. No answer. She used the spare key Odile had entrusted to her two years earlier, “just in case”. She found Odile in bed, burning with fever, trying to get up and saying she was late for the greenhouse.

Dr Martin came within the hour. Bronchitis, he said, probably because of the mistral. Nothing serious, provided she rested. Three weeks in bed, at least. No train, no greenhouse, no planting. Odile listened to the diagnosis with the expression of a queen being told she must abdicate. “And Strasbourg?” she asked. “It’s on the 25th.”

“Even if the planting were in the next street,” Dr Martin replied, “you wouldn’t go.” Odile closed her eyes. Julien, who was there, sat on the edge of the bed. He proposed a compromise: Amina would take a tablet, and Odile would attend the planting by video, from her bed. Odile opened one eye. “Whatever the picture quality,” she said, “I want to see the label.”

On Saturday 25 October, in Strasbourg, it was pouring. The planting took place in the little garden of the former chapel, on the banks of the Ill. Mrs Keller had brought the municipal brass band, who played under umbrellas. Amina held the tablet at arm’s length, protected by a plastic bag, and on the screen you could see Odile in bed, in her nightdress, her glasses on her nose.

Before planting the tree, Julien held the label up to the camera. “Strasbourg. Henri and Hélène, 1962.” On the screen Odile nodded, satisfied. Then she asked them to turn up the sound, and she whistled the three notes, from Lyon, in a rather weak voice. The Strasbourg band took it up, in the rain. The Alsatian children sang the melody, without words.

Julien glanced at Amina. She was still holding the tablet, but her face was wet, and it wasn’t only the rain. When she saw him looking at her, she looked away. “It’s the rain, Mr Moreau,” she said very quickly. “Only the rain. It isn’t an emotion.” Julien said nothing. He wrote the date in his notebook.

In Lille, on 8 November, it was cold and grey. Mrs Vandamme came to the planting with a cardboard box under her arm. Inside was an old dented cornet, tarnished by the years. It was her father’s, the miner’s, the one who had played in the mine’s brass band. She had kept it for forty years in a cupboard, without ever opening it. She gave it to a ten-year-old boy, the shyest in the orchestra.

It took the boy twenty minutes to get a sound out of it. But when he managed it, Mrs Vandamme closed her eyes, like Mrs Roux in Villeurbanne when she heard Lucien’s clarinet. Julien thought that the project wasn’t only planting trees. It was bringing back to life instruments forgotten in cupboards, and memories forgotten in hearts.

Clermont-Ferrand, on the other hand, sent bad news. On 12 November the mayor wrote to the ministry that the city could not take part in the project, for lack of budget. Julien read the letter three times. However hard he looked for a solution, he found none. Nine cities out of ten was already a lot, Amina told him. But Julien was thinking of the tenth lime tree, waiting in the greenhouse.

A week later, a thick envelope arrived at the Croix-Rousse office. It came from a primary school in Clermont-Ferrand. Inside was a letter handwritten by a whole class, and sixty-three children’s signatures, some in clumsy letters, others with drawings. The letter simply said: “We want to play the waltz too. Even in the dark.”

Julien sent a copy of the letter to the mayor of Clermont-Ferrand, without comment. Three days later, the mayor called back. He had found an old closed school that could serve as a hall, and a local company willing to pay for the instruments. “Even if the city didn’t have a cent,” he said, “I can’t say no to sixty-three children. My own granddaughter signed.”

Amina moved the red pin for Clermont-Ferrand, which had been left to one side on the map, and stuck it in with the others. Ten out of ten. She opened a new spreadsheet, “Plantings spring 2031”, because it was too late to plant in winter. Then, without Julien asking her, she wrote in the margin, in pencil: “Find an olive post for Clermont. Just in case.”

All this time Odile had stayed in bed, as Dr Martin had ordered. Or rather, almost in bed. She got up every morning to open her door and listen to Rose-Hélène’s harmonica, then went back to bed. The bronchitis was slowly clearing. But Ioana had noticed that when Odile whistled the waltz in the evening, her voice was weaker than before, and she sometimes stopped halfway.

Isabelle came from Paris for three days as soon as she heard the news. She slept on her mother’s sofa, made soups, tidied the cupboards and tried, without success, to stop her getting up. “Mum, however much you say you’re fine, you’re nearly eighty, and you have bronchitis.” Odile looked at her over her glasses. “My girl, even if I were a hundred, I would get up to listen to that little one.”

Rose-Hélène came to see her every afternoon, after the crèche. She sat on the bed with her harmonica and asked for stories. Odile told her about the storms Henri had sailed through, the distant ports, the flying fish of the Indian Ocean. Rose-Hélène listened with her mouth open. Then she always asked the same question: “And afterwards, did he come back?” Odile always answered yes.

Ioana, for her part, was six months pregnant. Her belly had grown round, and the baby moved a lot, especially in the evening, especially when Rose-Hélène played the harmonica. She had cut down her hours at the office. Nathalie had insisted. “Whatever you say,” she declared, “you’ll work three days a week until January. That’s an order from your boss. And from your partner.” Ioana didn’t dare argue.

On Tuesday 25 November, late in the afternoon, Odile sent for Julien. She was sitting in her armchair by the window, wrapped in her shawl. On her lap was the little notebook in which she had written down, all summer, Mr Fournier’s advice on caring for the lime trees. She handed it to him without a word.

“What’s this?” Julien asked, though he knew. “My notes,” Odile replied. “For the spring plantings. In case I can’t come.” Julien wanted to protest, to tell her she would come, that she would go to Clermont, to Toulouse, to Nantes, everywhere. She stopped him with a wave of her hand, gently, the way you stop a child who is talking too fast.

“Stubborn as I may be, Julien, I’m not eternal,” she said. “I’ll be eighty in a month. I’m not saying I’m going to leave. I’m only saying that, whatever happens, the lime trees must be planted. And whoever plants them must know that you water them in the evening, never at midday, and that you talk to them a little. Mr Fournier says it’s pointless. I say it works.”

Julien took the notebook. He opened it. On the first page, Odile had written in her large slanting hand: “Trees, like people, need someone to wait for them.” He closed the notebook and put it in the inside pocket of his jacket, next to his own notebook. Then he stayed sitting beside her until nightfall, without speaking, looking at the roofs of the Croix-Rousse.

That evening, when he went back home across the landing, he heard, through Odile’s door, the first three notes of the waltz. Faint, a little shaky, but in tune. He stopped for a moment in the corridor. Then he answered, whistling the next three notes. Behind the door there was a little laugh. Then silence. Then the light went out.

In the mistral, the minister gives a very short speech. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.

Ladies and gentlemen, dear children. I had prepared a ten-minute speech. But however talented my advisers may be, I don’t think the mistral will let me read it. So I will be brief, although that goes against every ministerial tradition.

This lime tree comes from Lyon. It grew from a tree under which, in 1962, two young people kissed for the first time. They never married. They never even saw each other again. Yet their story has come all the way here, to L’Estaque.

Wherever you live in France, in a big city or a small village, by the sea or in the mountains, you have the right to learn music. Whoever your parents are, whatever your means, an instrument is waiting for you.
Minister though I am, I can’t play the waltz. But I know one thing: even if this project cost more than planned, it would be worth it. Figures are forgotten. Trees remain.

I now give the floor to the most important person of this morning. She is seventy-nine, she carried this lime tree on her lap from Lyon, and, despite the wind and despite her doctor, she insisted on planting it herself. Mrs Odile Bernard.

Odile made no speech. She took the shovel, threw three shovelfuls of earth at the foot of the lime tree, and whistled the first three notes of the waltz. The wind carried the whistle out to sea. Nobody knew whether it had arrived anywhere. But everyone applauded.
